### introDuction **•** **_Arguably one of the most significant developments in January was the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. From this emerged the “Statement” which projected that economic conditions “are likely to warrant exceptionally low levels for the federal funds rate at least through late 2014”. All the precious metals rallied during January, but this Statement boosted prices further, especially gold, as it revitalised expectations not just for a protracted period of negative real interest rates, but also reminded the markets of inflationary pressures for the medium term._** **•** **_While gold needs to pause for breath after its early February attack on $1,760, we continue to expect gold to challenge $2,000 before the end of this year as investors, both at the “grass roots” and at the professional level, continue to hedge against fiat currency and financial risk. Political tensions have still not abated in the Gulf and this may also help to inform investor sentiment. The combination of higher gold prices and continued economic stress suggests that the balance of demand will continue its shift from jewellery towards investment products. It is possible that this price strength will be sustained through into early 2013 before investor appetite becomes stated._** **•** **_Silver continues to sustain a surplus and the prospect for higher prices therefo

re remains dependent on investment interest. While uncertainties hang over the global economy, and with the sharp price falls of 2011 still clear in investors’ minds, this means that silver is still reliant on gold for any sustainable upside. The recent recovery to $35 may be enough for now. For the long term, with gold challenging $2,000, silver should move back above $45 by the end of this year._** **•** **_Platinum is also in surplus, but market sentiment has recently been focusing on supply-side issues that have helped a sharp recovery towards $1,650 at the start of 2012. That said, expected short-term weakness in gold may offset (platinum) supply-side related support. For the longer term, renewed interest in gold may well spill into the platinum market, prompting a test of $1,790 before year-end._** **•** **_Palladium remains the most robust metal in the sector and has now been rising for more than four months to trade above $730. With the market entering a long-term deficit a test of $880 is foreseeable before year-end, with further strength developing in 2013. House prices have been falling, consumer confidence has been on the retreat again and the leading economic indicator index for December was just 0.4% against expectations of 0.9%. Fourth quarter GDP showed growth of 2.8%, but much of this was inventory rebuilding, with retail sales within the united states posting growth of just 0.9%. in his testimony to congress in early February, Federal reserve chairman Bernanke defended the Fed’s ultra low interest rate policy, stating that the eu crisis was still putting the us recovery under pressure and that the Fed would do everything possible to avoid contagion. He cited low inflation, slow industrial growth and the “fact that the dollar is a safe haven” as part of the elements informing the low interest rate policy. He robustly parried a suggestion from the chairman of the House Budget committee that the Fed’s post-Fomc statement hinted that it might be prepared to allow inflation to drift above 2%, insisting that the Fed would not tolerate higher inflation. Furthermore the latest ecB survey of lending conditions suggests that credit conditions are likely to tighten further in this quarter. This, in principle, argues that the dollar will remain a key safe haven over the coming months while the destiny of the euro remains uncertain. although this argues in part against a bull market for gold, the other elements of fiscal and economic uncertainty point towards fresh investment activity in the gold market over the months to come. **I3** Precious meTals oNe moNTH relaTive PerFormaNce February 2012 - IntroductIon confidential - not for distribution

The boost that these gave gold was exceeded by that accorded to silver partly because of ratio trading, and partly due to short covering activity. Platinum’s rally has been bolstered by concerns over mine supply even though the market has plenty of liquidity, while palladium’s continued recovery is justified by long-term fundamentals._ _From the start of February 2011 to early February 2012 gold has been the clear outperformer as rising concerns over the Eurozone have boosted risk hedging while putting something of a cloud over industrial metals. ### GolD **•** **_Gold staged a strong recovery in January after December’s low fix of $1,531, posted on the afternoon of the 29th, before closing the year at $1,574.50. The final fix of January (and the first fix of February) was $1,744, representing a gain of 10.8% and unwinding 61.1% of the fall from the early September 2011 high of $1,879.50._** **•** **_This is almost exactly a classic Fibonacci 61.8% retracement of the September-December fall and adds further strength to our view that the gold price needs a period of consolidation during February. The physical market has helped to support the rally, especially in China, while Indian activity has been mixed, but appears to be improving. There are some signs of scrap selling appearing from parts of East Asia and the Middle East in early February._** **•** **_We continue to expect strong investment activity during 2012 as the markets hedge against fiat currency risk and longer-term inflationary pressures. The recent statement from the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), in which it projects ultra low federal funds rates through to late 2014, a year later than had previously been expected, adds further fuel to this argument. Before the United States-oriented development, the emphasis on investment in January appears to have lain with Europe with little tangible activity in the United States (apart from coin sales); then there was a surge in investment in US-listed ETFs in the wake of the FOMC meeting._** **•** **_A challenge of $2,000 towards the end of the year is likely and strength should be sustained into 2013, but it is doubtful that investor appetite will be sustained for much of the year. As this activity starts to wane then gold prices should start to decline._** recent price action; a slowing in momentum may well lead to a correction The january rally in prices started strongly, with a range of more than $40 on the first day of trading, taking gold over $1,600. This swift move was not prompted by anything specific, although the dollar was weakening, investors were bargain hunting and commodities as a whole were trading higher in response to improving confidence over the economic outlook. There was liquidation in the eTFs in early january, but this was quickly reversed. The markets’ initial confidence about eco

nomic improvement was short-lived, and gold then advanced steadily for much of the month on risk-hedging activity, reaching almost $1,680 on 23rd january. Weakening economic data from the united states was taken to be supportive as it suggested an extended period of low interest rates and the likelihood of Qe3. Gold’s steady gains were quickened on the 25th january when gold bounded higher, adding more than $60 in response to the Fomc statement and the upward momentum continued thereafter. Part of the strength of gold’s move on 25th january was also technically-driven. During that day gold broke up above resistance that had been offered by a trend of declining highs stemming back to early september; furthermore the late November / early Decemb

er price fall had severed the medium-term uptrend that started in February 2011 (and which was briefly broken in september). The rally in late january saw this uptrend regained. The technical picture also improved in late january with the “Golden cross”, which is when the 20-day moving average crosses the 50-day to the upside and is widely regarded as a strong bull signal. Price outlook; time for a correction and consolidation before renewing the upward trend The price action in january, especially with the reattainment of the medium-term uptrend, means that, on a chart construction at least, gold now has support at $1,700-1,710, then there is strong support between $1,665 and $1,670. The market is overbought at prices above $1,740 and is due for a correction and, with the physical market also slowing after the recent strength, there is a strong possibility of a retreat towards these lower levels. Furthermore, the likelihood of a partial recovery in the us dollar in the near term, along with the effects of a market “straved” of liquidity (in spite of the ecB’s efforts to alleviate this problem), could see gold in fact fall below $1,600 before the end of march. Nevertheless, looking further ahead, the prospects for price appreciation will again depend on investment interest this year. key drivers obviously include: - **_the extremely low level of interest rates in the United States, and the likelihood of more interest rate cuts from the European Central Bank, especially in combination with the high (and rising) level of liquidity in the financial system;_** - **_the associated longer-term inflationary pressures;_** ###### GolD iN local Terms, sHorT Term GolD iN major curreNcies, meDium Term 115

Although Chinese headline inflation has been falling, and reduced export demand is helping to slow China’s rate of growth, the local population remains fearful of rising prices;_** - **_Continued publicity surrounding central bank acquisitions and the impact that this has on market sentiment as it highlights the possibility of continued stresses in the currency markets and financial system;_** The euro’s rally against the dollar was helpful to gold in january although the metal had a momentum of its own Gold’s rise from the late-December low through to the high trade at the end of january (on an intra-day basis) was 13.7%. The increase in euro terms was slightly smaller, at 12.5%, reflecting a net strengthening of the euro against the dollar during january. Given that the eurozone is a focus of concern in the financial markets, this may seem counter-intuitive, but in fact the euro had dropped by 16% against the dollar between early may and mid-january. The rally is therefore partly a correction from a mediumterm downtrend, extended by the market’s reaction to the Fomc’s interest rate statement. The gain in rupee terms was more constrained, at just 7% as the rupee regained some of the strength that it had lost in the fourth quarter of last year.
